t: Launched by the Edict of Gülhane in 1839, the Tanzimat promised all Ottoman subjects security of life, property and honour, fair taxation and conscription, public trials and an end to tax farming.

Statesmen of the Sublime Porte such as Mustafa Reşid Pasha, Âli Pasha and Fuad Pasha rebuilt the ministries, courts, schools, law codes and army, and promoted Ottomanism, the equality of all subjects.

The reforms culminated in the constitution of 1876 but left the empire bankrupt, while Balkan separatism, conservative opposition and foreign intervention grew; historians still dispute whether they strengthened the state or hastened its break-up.
dyk: The Ottoman penal code of 1858, modelled on France’s Napoleonic Code, abolished punishments such as amputation of a limb for theft and decriminalized homosexuality; it endured until 1928.
ev: Mahmud II destroys the Janissaries in the Auspicious Incident, opening a period of Western-style reform and centralization
Sultan Abdulmejid I issues the Edict of Gülhane, guaranteeing all subjects security of life, honour and property and abolishing tax farming
The Imperial Reform Edict promises full legal equality for citizens of all religions and abolishes the jizya
The Land Code and a penal code modelled on the Napoleonic Code are promulgated
The Vilayet Law reorganizes the provinces and the secular Nizamiye Courts are established
A Nationality Law creates a common Ottoman citizenship irrespective of religion
Foreign borrowing ends in bankruptcy, and tax grievances help spark the Herzegovina Uprising
Midhat Pasha’s Ottoman Constitution sets up a Senate and a Chamber of Deputies, closing the Tanzimat

f.where: The Ottoman Empire: Istanbul and the provinces, among them the Balkans, Bosnia, Herzegovina, Mount Lebanon and Palestine.
f.period: Built on Mahmud II’s reforms after 1826; opened by the Edict of Gülhane (1839); renewed by the Imperial Reform Edict (1856); the Vilayet Law and the Nizamiye Courts (1864); a period of chaos after Âli Pasha’s death (1871); closed by the constitution of 1876 amid the Great Eastern Crisis (1875–1878).
f.figures: Mustafa Reşid Pasha, former ambassador to London and Paris; the reforming statesmen Mehmed Emin Âli Pasha and Fuad Pasha; Sultans Abdul Mejid I and Abdul Aziz; Midhat Pasha, author of the 1876 constitution; the Young Ottomans, a secret society of reformers.
f.outcome: A conscripted army, new ministries, schools and universities, secular courts and codes, the Mecelle, railways, telegraphs and banks, and the constitution of 1876; but also bankruptcy in 1875, foreign control of revenues from 1881, Balkan risings and the losses of the Treaty of Berlin (1878).
